title: Part 1, Chapter 45
paragraphs: In which the doubtful question of Mambrino's helmet and the pack-saddle is finally settled, with other adventures that occurred in truth and earnest
"What do you all think now, gentlemen," said the barber, "of what these fine gentlemen are saying when they try to make out that this is a helmet?"
"And anyone who says the opposite," said Don Quixote, "I'll let him know he lies — if he's a knight; and if he's a squire, that he lies a thousand times over."

Our own barber, who had been present through all of this and understood Don Quixote's brand of madness perfectly, decided to back up the delusion and keep the joke going for everyone's amusement; so turning to the other barber he said:

"Señor barber, or whatever you are, you should know that I belong to your profession too. I've held a licence to practise for more than twenty years, and I know every implement of the barber's craft inside out. I was also a soldier for a time in my youth, so I know what a helmet is, and a morion, and a headpiece with a visor, and the other gear of soldiering — I mean to say, of soldiers' arms. And I say — saving better opinions and always deferring to sounder judgments — that this piece in front of us, which this worthy gentleman has in his hands, not only is not a barber's basin, but is as far from being one as white is from black, or truth from falsehood. I'll add that this, although it is a helmet, is not a complete helmet."
"Certainly not," said Don Quixote, "because half of it is missing — the beaver, that is."

"Quite true," said the curate, who could see what his friend the barber was up to. Cardenio, Don Fernando, and his companions agreed, and even the Judge would have helped carry on the joke if his mind hadn't been so occupied with Don Luis's situation; but the serious matter weighing on him left him paying little or no attention to these comic proceedings.

"God help me!" exclaimed the barber, the butt of all this. "Is it possible that such an honourable company can say this is not a basin but a helmet? Why, this would astonish an entire university, however learned. Enough — if this basin is a helmet, then the pack-saddle must be a horse's caparison, as this gentleman has said."
"To me it looks like a pack-saddle," said Don Quixote, "but I've already said I will not get involved in that question."
"Whether it's a pack-saddle or a caparison," said the curate, "is for Señor Don Quixote to decide; for in matters of chivalry all of us gentlemen bow to his authority."

"By God, gentlemen," said Don Quixote, "so many strange things have happened to me in this castle during the two visits I've made that I won't venture to assert anything positively about anything in it. It's my belief that everything that goes on here happens by enchantment. The first time, an enchanted Moor who lives here gave me a great deal of trouble, and Sancho didn't fare well with certain followers of his either. And last night I was left hanging by this arm for nearly two hours, with no idea how or why such a thing came to pass. So for me to step forward now and give an opinion on so puzzling a matter would be reckless. As for the claim that this is a basin and not a helmet, I've already answered. But on the question of whether this is a pack-saddle or a caparison, I won't venture a firm opinion — I'll leave it to your worships' better judgment. Perhaps, since you've not been dubbed knights as I have, the enchantments of this place have no hold on you, your faculties are unfettered, and you can see things in this castle as they really and truly are, rather than as they appear to me."

"There can be no question," said Don Fernando, "that Señor Don Quixote has spoken very wisely, and that the decision rests with us. And so we may have surer ground to go on, I'll take the gentlemen's votes in secret and announce the result clearly and fully."

To those who were in on the joke about Don Quixote's mania this was all great fun, but to those who knew nothing about it, it seemed the most absurd nonsense in the world — particularly to Don Luis's four servants, to Don Luis himself, and to three other travellers who had chanced to arrive at the inn and looked like officers of the Holy Brotherhood, which is in fact what they were. But the one who was most at his wits' end was the barber whose basin, in front of his very eyes, had turned into Mambrino's helmet, and whose pack-saddle, he had no doubt, was about to become a rich horse's caparison. Everyone laughed to see Don Fernando going from one to another collecting votes and whispering to them to give their private opinion on whether the much-fought-over treasure was a pack-saddle or a caparison. After he had taken the votes of those who knew Don Quixote, he said aloud, "The fact is, my good fellow, I'm tired of collecting opinions, because there isn't one of those I've asked who doesn't tell me it's absurd to say this is the pack-saddle of an ass and not the caparison of a horse — indeed, of a thoroughbred horse. So you'll have to submit; for, in spite of you and your ass, this is a caparison and no pack-saddle, and you have stated and proved your case very poorly."

"May I never see heaven," said the poor barber, "if your worships aren't all mistaken. May my soul appear before God just as that thing appears to me to be a pack-saddle and not a caparison. But — 'laws go as kings like' — I'll say no more. And no, I'm not drunk: I'm fasting, except from sin."
The barber's simple talk was no less amusing than Don Quixote's absurdities, and Don Quixote now observed:
"There's nothing more to be done now than for each man to take what belongs to him, and to whom God has given it, may St. Peter add his blessing."

But one of the four servants said, "Unless this is a deliberate joke, I cannot bring myself to believe that men as intelligent as those here are, or appear to be, would dare declare and assert that this is not a basin and that not a pack-saddle. But since I see they are declaring it, I can only conclude there's some mystery in their insisting on what so plainly contradicts experience and the truth itself. By" — and here he let out a round oath — "all the people in the world won't make me believe that this is not a barber's basin and that not a jackass's pack-saddle."
"It might just as easily be a she-ass's," observed the curate.
"It's all the same," said the servant. "That's not the point. The point is whether it is or isn't a pack-saddle, as your worships are saying."

Hearing this, one of the newly arrived officers of the Brotherhood, who had been listening to the dispute, lost his patience and exclaimed, "It is a pack-saddle, as sure as my father is my father, and whoever has said or will say anything else must be drunk."

"You lie like a rascally clown," Don Quixote shot back; and lifting his pike, which he had never let out of his hand, he aimed such a blow at the man's head that, had the officer not dodged it, he would have been laid out flat. The pike shattered against the ground. The rest of the officers, seeing their comrade attacked, raised a shout calling for help for the Holy Brotherhood. The landlord, who was a member of the fraternity, ran at once to fetch his staff of office and his sword and lined up with his comrades. Don Luis's servants clustered around him so he couldn't slip away in the confusion. The barber, seeing the house in uproar, grabbed his pack-saddle again, and Sancho did the same. Don Quixote drew his sword and charged the officers. Don Luis was shouting at his servants to leave him alone and go help Don Quixote, while Cardenio and Don Fernando backed Don Quixote up. The curate was yelling at the top of his lungs, the landlady screaming, her daughter wailing, Maritornes weeping, Dorothea aghast, Luscinda terror-stricken, and Doña Clara in a faint. The barber clubbed Sancho, and Sancho pummelled the barber. Don Luis gave one of his servants — who had grabbed his arm to keep him from escaping — a clout that bloodied his teeth. The Judge took his part. Don Fernando had one of the officers on the ground and was thrashing him soundly. The landlord shouted again for help for the Holy Brotherhood. The whole inn was nothing but cries, shouts, shrieks, confusion, terror, dismay, mishaps, sword-cuts, fisticuffs, cudgellings, kicks, and bloodshed. And in the middle of all this chaos and tangle, Don Quixote took it into his head that he had been dropped right into the thick of the discord of Agramante's camp; and in a voice that shook the inn like thunder he cried out:
"Stop, everyone! Let everyone sheathe his sword, let everyone be calm and listen to me, as you value your lives!"

Everyone paused at the force of his voice, and he went on, "Did I not tell you, sirs, that this castle was enchanted, and that a legion of devils dwelt in it? As proof I call on you to see with your own eyes how the discord of Agramante's camp has come here and been transferred into the middle of us. Look how they fight — there for the sword, here for the horse, over there for the eagle, on this side for the helmet; we are all fighting, and all at cross purposes. Come then, you, Señor Judge, and you, señor curate — let the one stand as King Agramante and the other as King Sobrino, and make peace among us. By God Almighty, it is a sorry thing that so many people of quality as we are should kill one another over such trifles." The officers, who did not understand Don Quixote's manner of speaking and found themselves roughly handled by Don Fernando, Cardenio, and their companions, were not about to be appeased. The barber was, however, since both his beard and his pack-saddle were the worse for the struggle. Sancho, like a good servant, obeyed his master's slightest word, while Don Luis's four servants kept quiet when they saw how little they gained by being otherwise. The landlord alone insisted they must punish the insolence of this madman, who at every turn raised an uproar in the inn. But at length the disturbance was stilled for the time being. In Don Quixote's imagination the pack-saddle remained a caparison until the day of judgment, the basin a helmet, and the inn a castle.

Once everyone had been calmed and reconciled by the Judge's and the curate's persuasion, Don Luis's servants began again to press him to return home with them at once. While he was arguing with them, the Judge took counsel with Don Fernando, Cardenio, and the curate about what he should do, telling them how things stood and what Don Luis had said to him. It was finally agreed that Don Fernando would tell Don Luis's servants who he was, and that it was his wish that Don Luis accompany him to Andalusia, where Don Luis would receive from his brother the marquis the welcome his rank deserved; for otherwise it was clear from Don Luis's determination that he wouldn't return to his father right now, even if they tore him to pieces. On learning Don Fernando's rank and Don Luis's resolve, the four settled it among themselves: three of them would go back to tell his father how matters stood, and the fourth would stay to wait on Don Luis and not leave him until they returned to fetch him or his father's orders arrived. So by the authority of Agramante and the wisdom of King Sobrino this whole tangle of disputes was arranged. But the enemy of concord and hater of peace, feeling himself slighted and made a fool of, and seeing how little he'd gained after weaving them all into so elaborate an entanglement, resolved to try his hand once more by stirring up fresh quarrels and disturbances.

It came about this way. The officers were pacified once they learned the rank of those they'd been fighting, and withdrew from the contest, judging that whatever the outcome they were likely to come off the worse. But one of them — the one Don Fernando had thrashed and kicked — remembered that among the warrants he carried for the arrest of various criminals he had one against Don Quixote, whom the Holy Brotherhood had ordered arrested for freeing the galley slaves, exactly as Sancho had very reasonably feared. Suspecting this, he wanted to confirm whether Don Quixote's features matched the description. Taking a parchment out of his coat, he found what he was looking for, and setting himself to read it slowly — because he was no quick reader — he fixed his eyes on Don Quixote with each word, comparing the description in the warrant with his face, and concluded that beyond any doubt this was the man named in it. Once satisfied, he folded up the parchment, took the warrant in his left hand, and with his right grabbed Don Quixote by the collar so tightly that he could hardly breathe, and shouted, "Help for the Holy Brotherhood! And to show you I'm serious, read this warrant, which says this highwayman is to be arrested."

The curate took the warrant and saw that what the officer said was true, and that it matched Don Quixote's appearance. Don Quixote, finding himself roughly handled by this rascally clown, was worked up to the highest pitch of fury, every joint cracking with rage. With both hands he seized the officer by the throat with all his strength, so that had his comrades not come to his aid he would have given up his life before Don Quixote let go. The landlord, who was bound to support his fellow officers, ran at once to help them. The landlady, seeing her husband caught up in yet another fight, again raised her voice, and Maritornes and the daughter immediately joined her, calling on heaven and everyone present for help. Sancho, watching all this, exclaimed, "By the Lord, what my master says about the enchantments of this castle is true — it's impossible to live an hour in peace here!"

Don Fernando separated the officer and Don Quixote, and to their mutual relief made them release their grip — the one on the coat collar, the other on his adversary's throat. Even so, the officers did not stop demanding their prisoner and calling on the others to help them and hand him over bound, as was required for the service of the King and of the Holy Brotherhood, on whose behalf they once more demanded aid in capturing this robber and footpad of the highways.

Don Quixote smiled when he heard these words and said very calmly, "Come now, you base, ill-born brood — do you call it highway robbery to give freedom to those in bondage, to release captives, to help the wretched, to raise up the fallen, to relieve the needy? You infamous creatures, whose vile, grovelling intellects deserve that heaven should never reveal to you the virtue that lies in knight-errantry, nor show you the sin and ignorance in which you wallow when you refuse to respect even the shadow, let alone the presence, of any knight-errant. Come on then — band, not of officers, but of thieves, footpads licensed by the Holy Brotherhood: tell me, who was the fool that signed an arrest warrant against such a knight as I am? Who didn't know that knights-errant are independent of all jurisdictions, that their law is their sword, their charter their prowess, and their edicts their will? Who, I ask again, was the dolt who doesn't know that there are no patents of nobility that confer such privileges or exemptions as a knight-errant acquires the day he is dubbed and devotes himself to the demanding calling of chivalry? What knight-errant ever paid poll-tax, duty, queen's pin-money, king's dues, toll, or ferry? What tailor ever made him pay for his clothes? What castellan who received him in his castle ever made him pay his bill? What king did not seat him at his table? What damsel did not fall in love with him and surrender herself wholly to his will and pleasure? And finally, what knight-errant has there ever been, or is there, or will there ever be in the world who isn't bold enough single-handedly to give four hundred cudgellings to four hundred officers of the Holy Brotherhood if they cross his path?"
